prompt: In object oriented programming, what is a class?
choices: A single object that already holds real data
A blueprint that describes the attributes and methods its objects will have
A function stored inside a module for later reuse
A variable that can hold only one value at a time
explain: A class is the blueprint. The objects you create from it are the instances that hold the actual data.

prompt: What is the job of the __init__ method?
choices: It runs automatically when a new object is made and sets up that object's attributes
It deletes the object once the program finishes
It must be called by hand after the object has been created
It defines the class variables that every object will share
explain: Python calls __init__ for you as soon as the object is created, and its usual job is assigning the starting attributes.

code:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a = Dog("Buddy")
b = Dog("Max")
a.name = "Rex"
print(b.name)
choices: Rex
Buddy
It raises an error because name was changed
Max
explain: Each object keeps its own instance variables, so renaming a leaves b.name as "Max".

prompt: What does the parameter self refer to inside a method?
choices: The class itself, so you can read class variables
The name of the method that is currently running
A copy of the object that is thrown away when the method ends
The specific object the method was called on
explain: Python passes the object itself as the first argument, so self is the particular instance the method is acting on.

choices: It raises a TypeError because accelerate takes no arguments
explain: Each call to accelerate adds 10 to the same object's speed attribute, so two calls give 20.

code:
class Counter:
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, label):
        self.label = label
        Counter.count += 1

c1 = Counter("first")
c2 = Counter("second")
c3 = Counter("third")
print(Counter.count)
choices: It raises a NameError because count is not defined with self
explain: count is a class variable shared by every instance, and each __init__ call adds one to it.

prompt: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a class variable and an instance variable?
choices: Class variables are private, instance variables are public
A class variable is shared by every object of the class, while each object has its own copy of an instance variable
Class variables can only hold numbers, instance variables can hold any type
Instance variables are defined at the top of the class, class variables are defined inside __init__
explain: Class variables live on the class and are shared, while instance variables are set with self and belong to one object.

code:

    kingdom = "Plantae"

p = Plant()

p.kingdom = "Fungi"
print(p.kingdom, q.kingdom, Plant.kingdom)

explain: Assigning p.kingdom creates a new instance variable that hides the class variable for p only, so q and the class still see "Plantae".

prompt: What does encapsulation mean in OOP?
choices: Writing a class that inherits from several parents at once
Bundling data and the methods that work on it together, and controlling how that data is reached from outside
Giving two different classes methods with the same name
Splitting a program into separate files so it is easier to read
explain: Encapsulation keeps an object's data and behaviour together and routes outside access through methods.

prompt: What does a single leading underscore, as in self._balance, signal to another programmer?
choices: That Python will refuse to let outside code read the attribute
That the attribute is a class variable rather than an instance variable
That the attribute is meant for internal use, by convention only
That the attribute is a constant that must never change
explain: A single underscore is only a convention meaning "internal". Python still allows direct access.

To stop a subclass from inheriting anything from its parent
explain: Overriding means the subclass supplies its own version of an inherited method under the same name.
